sources.title: Nvidia interim CEO Kress tells employees ‘let’s move forward’ at first all-hands meeting since Jensen Huang exit
sources.text: Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress told employees "let's move forward" on Wednesday during the company's first all-hands meeting since founder Jensen Huang resigned, a person who attended the meeting told CNBC. The person asked not to be named because the meeting was private. Kress was joined by newly appointed board chair Harvey Jones and hyperscale and high-performance computing head Ian Buck. Several other senior members of Nvidia's executive team spoke or joined Kress on stage, including longtime company veteran Jeff Fisher, senior vice president of software engineering Dwight Diercks, senior vice president of GPU engineering Jonah Alben, executive vice president in charge of operations Debora Shoquist and co-founder Chris Malachowsky, according to people familiar with the matter. Kress opened with the message about moving forward and also mentioned pay raises and explained that the yearly review process, when employees typically get pay raises and are granted more stock, would be moved up from March to December. Nvidia shares are down 37% from their 52-week high. Jones discussed the search for the next CEO, the person who attended the meeting said. The meeting lasted about an hour and was in person as well as streamed on Microsoft Teams. The general sentiment swirling in the room, according to the person, was that employees want Huang to come back . Employees have spoken up on X in recent days to call for the return of Huang as CEO, and one senior employee reportedly sent a letter to the board warning Nvidia would lose "irreplaceable talent" if it doesn't consider reinstating Huang. But another person familiar with the matter disagreed, saying that employees welcomed the remarks from leadership as well as the visibility into company leadership. The person asked not to be named because the matter is private. "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Jones said during the company's earnings call on Tuesday. Some executives shared that they do not agree with Jones. "Why make such a strong definitive statement when the investigation is still playing out," an employee told CNBC. The employee asked not to be named given the sensitivity of the subject. The meeting was held one day after Huang said he was ready to return as CEO should the board want him. Multiple employees told CNBC that Huang's letter "fired employees up." Despite recent turmoil, Wednesday's meeting was not out of the ordinary. Nvidia typically holds all-hands the morning after quarterly earnings reports, according to a former employee, who asked not to be named because the matter is private. Kress recapped Tuesday's earnings report, calling it a "great quarter," according to the person who said employees welcomed the remarks and visibility from leadership. In past meetings, Huang took time to answer questions submitted by employees, according to the former employee. A person familiar with the matter told CNBC that the executives also answered pre-submitted questions in Wednesday's all-hands. Nvidia shares were down Wednesday, a day after the company reported third-quarter earnings that topped Wall Street expectations and gave no signal that the company was going to slow its growth. Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that executives at Nvidia's all-hands meeting answered employee questions. A previous version mischaracterized how executives handled employee questions. WATCH: The rise, reinvention and uncertain future of Nvidia without Jensen Huang

sources.name: Fortune
sources.title: Nvidia can run without Jensen Huang. Can the AI boom?
sources.text: Welcome to Eye on AI. Beatrice Nolan here. In today’s issue: In October, Jeremy Kahn and I sat down with Jensen Huang during his European tour. At the time, Huang looked less like a chip executive and more like the AI boom’s chief evangelist. His word moved markets, his keynotes filled arenas, and his company was at one point worth more than $5.7 trillion. A month later, he was gone. For Fortune’s December/January magazine, we spoke with dozens of people to find out how Huang built his empire and what happens to it without him. In a wide-ranging interview (before news of the scandal broke), Huang defended the company’s complex web of financing. Nvidia pours money into startups, AI labs, and cloud companies, which in part use that money to buy Nvidia chips. Critics called this process “circular financing,” saying it leaves much of the AI boom dangerously exposed to weak links that could topple the entire house of cards. At that time, though, not even the company’s harshest critics thought the weak link could be the man at the center of it all: Huang. The scandal took about two weeks to unfold. Reports emerged that U.S. officials believed Huang had been romantically involved with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Singapore neocloud Megaspeed whom they suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. Huang admitted to staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife. Then the New York Times reported a second affair, with an Nvidia executive who had reported directly to him. Congress summoned him, federal agencies opened investigations, and on Nov. 12, under pressure from the board, he resigned after 33 years in charge. This seismic change to Nvidia exposed just how much the company rested on Huang. Nvidia had no president, no COO, and no obvious No. 2. In the immediate wake of his resignation, the board appointed CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, but few thought she was likely to get the job permanently. And that same dependence on Nvidia’s singular founder could be said of the entire AI boom. Under Huang, the company was happy to play the role of the AI industry’s central bank. It poured nearly $50 billion into model makers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI, and pledged around $170 billion in financing commitments. It’s unclear whether this will continue with quite the same momentum without Huang at the helm. In fact, there are already rumblings about Nvidia’s interim CEO Kress’s enthusiasm for some of Huang’s more outlandish investments. Kress said on Nvidia’s earnings call earlier this week—the first ever without Huang at the helm—that the company would be more “disciplined” and “rigorous” in assessing investments into the AI ecosystem going forward. “We are proud of the role that we have played so far in supporting the ecosystem,” she said in the earnings call with analysts on Tuesday. “As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.” Nvidia will also feel Huang’s absence in Washington. The former CEO was Nvidia’s most effective lobbyist, close to President Donald Trump, and a relentless critic of export controls. Indeed, within days of his exit, the Commerce Department moved to close a loophole that let Chinese firms rent access to U.S. chips through overseas data centers, which is the business Megaspeed is suspected of running. This week brought the first test of life after Jensen. On Tuesday, Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, more than double a year earlier, and guided to around $130 billion for the current quarter. Interim CEO Kress told investors: “We’ve got this.” But shares slipped in response. The call did, however, seemingly close the door on any return to Nvidia for Huang. Pressure had been building from some areas of the tech world to reinstate him, as industry figures fretted that some of Huang’s deals would leave with him. Huang even broke his own silence, posting that he would be “honored” to return. But on the day of earnings, board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia does not intend to reinstate him. The earnings show the fundamentals of the machine Huang built can run without him. Whether some of the companies most dependent on Nvidia will continue to thrive is a harder question. Beatrice Nolan beatrice.nolan@fortune.com @beafreyanolan Anthropic stock pops 30% to $2 trillion market cap, in mega IPO —by Beatrice Nolan ‘A failure of implementation’: AI played a key role in some outages—but not in the way you might think — by Emily Forlini Anthropic prices IPO at $83 per share, giving it a $1.5 trillion valuation — by Alexei Oreskovic The Nvidia scandal fuels tougher China chip rules as Commerce targets Singapore and Malaysia —by Nicholas Gordon Robot cage fights and snorting nanoparticles: Notes from the ‘reality distortion field’ of Silicon Valley’s AI frontier — by Alexei Oreskovic Sunrun and Overview Energy CEOs say the answer to AI’s energy problem is already on the grid — by Allie Garfinkle Nvidia beats estimates in its first quarter without Jensen Huang. Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, up 103% from a year earlier and about $7 billion above analyst estimates. Profit topped $65 billion. Interim CEO Colette Kress said demand for the new Vera Rubin platform is “off to an explosive start.” Nvidia guided to roughly $130 billion for the current quarter, ahead of forecasts. That figure assumes no China compute revenue, and the quarter includes an extra week. Still, shares slipped after the report. OpenAI’s new flagship crosses its own self-improvement threshold. OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and the cheaper GPT-6.2 Sol on Tuesday, with Astra priced about 20% below its predecessor. According to the system card, Astra is the first model OpenAI has released externally that meets its “High” threshold for AI self-improvement. sources.title: Elon Musk defiende a Jensen Huang, ex-CEO de NVIDIA, con una comparación explosiva: "Es como echar a Michael Jordan de un equipo ganador"
sources.text: Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google. Elon Musk, director ejecutivo de Tesla, ha apoyado públicamente a Huang, envuelto en un escándalo por infidelidades que ha hecho tambalear la estabilidad y prosperidad de Nvidia. Elon Musk ha vuelto a decir públicamente que está totalmente volcado con Jensen Huang después de que salieran a la luz diferentes relaciones sentimentales extramatrimoniales del directivo de Nvidia, que se ha visto obligado a salir de la compañía en la que ha trabajado más de tres décadas y quien, además del CEO de Tesla, también cuenta con el apoyo de otros directivos de Silicon Valley . Esta vez, para hablar sobre la gran relevancia que tiene Huang en la firma de chips, Musk ha hecho una curiosa comparación : "Es como Michael Jordan en su mejor momento, en lo que significa para un equipo", ha añadido. Con el anuncio de su salida de Nvidia, varios líderes del sector han mostrado su apoyo hacia Huang . Entre ellos, Sam Altman, CEO de OpenAI, Tim Sweeney, consejero delegado de Epic Games, o Steve Chen, director técnico de YouTube. Todos ellos, además de centenares de personas que actualmente trabajan para Nvidia y otros accionistas, han firmado una carta en la que se pide su regreso con el siguiente lema: "Treinta y tres años merecen una respuesta. exigimos a la Junta Directiva de Nvidia que traigan de vuelta a Jensen". Elon Musk suele ser una de las voces discordantes del sector y esta vez también lo ha sido en lo que respecta al cambio de dirección de Nvidia, que ha asumido Colette Kress , hasta ahora directora financiera de la empresa de chips más potente del mundo. Esto, que ha supuesto un cambio histórico para la organización y que ha puesto en duda la estabilidad y la prosperidad económica de la compañía, ha sido objetivo de muchos analistas de tecnología, que apuntan a una posible caída en picado de la empresa. Según los datos de la Bolsa, razones no les faltan para asegurar esto, y también hay otros compañeros de Huang que sostienen que la no admisión del exdirectivo en Nvidia es un despropósito. Principalmente, por lo que él ha significado para la compañía. "Jensen es un viejo amigo mío", ha dicho Musk, insistiendo en que el que fuera director ejecutivo de Nvidia hasta hace solo unos días "es como Michael Jordan en su mejor momento, en cuanto a lo que significa para un equipo". "No hay nadie que pueda reemplazar a Jensen. Tiene relaciones de largo recorrido que se han forjado a lo largo de décadas y comprende la tecnología a la perfección. Su equipo lo adora, lo aprecia muchísimo y muchos de ellos están ahí gracias a él ", ha matizado Musk en la cumbre Dealbook del New York Times. Tal y como indican desde TechCrunch , en este encuentro, Musk ha dejado caer que las personas que forman parte de Nvidia le tienen una gran estima y que esas relaciones humanas son las que han sostenido a la empresa hasta la fecha. "Han rechazado ofertas más lucrativas en otros lugares por lealtad personal a Jensen", ha sostenido en este encuentro, con una postura que también ha tomado el director ejecutivo de Anduril, Palmer Luckey. "China quiere que Jensen se vaya, así que yo quiero que se quede", explicó poco antes de la intervención de Musk, que también ha opinado acerca de las relaciones conocidas de Huang. Entre ellas, con la supuesta espía rusa Alice Huang. "No creo que sea desleal a Estados Unidos. Creo que es como echar a Michael Jordan de tu equipo cuando estás en racha ganadora y simplemente no parece algo bueno para los accionistas" , ha asegurado Musk. Esta opinión, no obstante, contrasta con la de Satya Nadella, líder de Microsoft, que ha subrayado también en este encuentro que, aunque la decisión final está en manos de la junta directiva, la nueva directora ejecutiva interina "es una persona extraordinaria". "Trabajó en Microsoft durante mucho tiempo y la conozco desde hace mucho. Tengo mucha confianza en el equipo de Nvidia para seguir haciendo un buen trabajo", ha asegurado Nadella.

sources.name: Fortune
sources.title: Anthropic stock pops 30% to $2 trillion market cap in mega IPO
sources.text: Anthropic’s stock surged more than 30% in first minutes as a public company, a roaring debut that crowned the AI company—at least briefly—with a stunning, $2 trillion market cap. Shares of Anthropic opened at $111.50 per share on Thursday, up 34% from the $83 IPO price. The stock pop began to moderate somewhat as the trading day continued, with shares trading up 14%, at $94.50 per share. Shares of Anthropic, under the ticker symbol “ANT,” began trading a couple of hours after the stock market’s opening bell. The strong demand for Anthropic shares came as the broader market was under pressure, with the Nasdaq down 363 points and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 1038 points in midday trading. At the $111.50 opening price, Anthropic’s market cap was roughly $2 trillion—an astounding Wall Street debut that instantly puts the five-year-old AI company in the elite club of trillion-dollar public companies. “This moment is bigger than any one company, or any one country. It will take all of us, working together, to ensure this technology goes well for us and the many generations to come,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in a statemen t posted on X on Thursday. Anthropic priced the offering Wednesday night at $83 a share , above its marketed range of $70 to $78, giving the company a $1.5 trillion valuation. Demand was strong enough that it raised the deal to 980 million shares from 825 million. There had been endless speculation about whether Anthropic would top SpaceX as the largest IPO of all time. At a $1.5 trillion IPO valuation, Anthropic would be the second most valuable IPO of all time, behind SpaceX’s $1.77 trillion IPO in June. Measured by capital raised however, Anthropic’s $79 billion ($81.4 billion, if stock sold by insiders is included) topped the $75 billion raised by SpaceX. Seven strategic partners, including Google and Nvidia , have also agreed to buy $26 billion of non-voting Anthropic stock at the IPO price. The deal’s underwriters also have a “greenshoe” option to purchase an additional 147 million shares of Anthropic stock. If exercised, that would bring the proceeds of Anthropic’s IPO to $118 billion. The offering will provide Anthropic with a vital infusion of capital as it seeks to stay ahead in the AI race and to invest in the computing infrastructure to train its models. It will also make instant billionaires out of numerous Anthropic employees and early investors, particularly the seven cofounders who created Anthropic. At least 400 early hires will be worth $100 million or more, according to CNBC. “Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” Amodei said in his statement Thursday. “We will not bend to either business or political pressure,” Amodei said, invoking the company’s stated commitment to develop AI technology with safeguards. Anticipation for the IPOs of Anthropic and its arch-rival OpenAI has been building ever since OpenAI ignited the generative AI boom in late 2022 with the launch of ChatGPT. With OpenAI holding off on its IPO until at least 2027, Anthropic becomes the first pure-play maker of frontier AI models to go public (SpaceX also does rockets, and Google and Meta both have massive businesses in search and social media). But the Anthropic IPO also comes at a tenuous time for the AI industry. It’s been barely a week since the AI industry lost one of its most powerful figures. Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO last Thursday , following reports that he had engaged in two extramarital affairs: one with a customer suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese intelligence asset, and one with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. His exit added fresh pressure to a listing that was already seen as a stress test of investors’ appetite for AI. Analysts and investors told Fortune they didn’t expect the Nvidia shock to derail the offering or touch Anthropic’s core business. The bigger risk, they said, may come later. Seaport Research Partners analyst Jay Goldberg warned that turmoil at Nvidia could bring Anthropic “much tougher questions” once it starts reporting quarterly results as a public company. Georgetown’s Jason Schloetzer predicted closer scrutiny of Anthropic’s ties to Nvidia and to customers associated with the chipmaker. Anthropic’s revenue has soared thanks to strong demand from business customers, a market in which Anthropic has been especially successfull. In the nine months ending September 30, Anthropic generated $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. The company posted a $104 billion net loss in its most recent nine-month period, though the bulk of the red ink is because of the way it accounted for its convertible notes. But the high share price straight out of the gates will put immense pressure on Anthropic as it seeks to justify its valuation to investors and to prove that AI tools can deliver the massive payoff Wall Street expects. Anthropic CEO Amodei, once the VP of research at OpenAI, left to cofound Anthropic at the end of 2020, along with sister Daniella and several other OpenAI employees, when they became disillusioned with OpenAI’s approach to AI safety. Still, the company’s IPO prospectus is replete with warnings of the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence including “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” The IPO also comes amid growing public backlash to AI data centers, underscored by the results of the U.S. midterm elections. High profile incidents of rogue AI agents, by OpenAI as well as Anthropic, have added to the unease over the technology. The stakes reach well beyond one company. Anthropic has more than 400 backers, and nearly every major venture firm owns a piece of it, so the IPO is effectively a liquidity event for the AI boom itself. sources.title: Anthropic IPO live updates: AI lab tops $2 trillion market cap, Ashton Kutcher celebrates debut
sources.text: This is CNBC live coverage of Anthropic's IPO and Nasdaq debut. Anthropic opened at $111.50 per share in the artificial intelligence lab's Nasdaq debut on Thursday after the company completed the biggest initial public offering on record. The stock will trade under the ticker "ANT" after the company raised $81.3 billion in the IPO. The Claude creator sold 980 million shares at $83 a piece on Wednesday, lifting the size and price of its offering. The 5-year-old company captivated the corporate world with its Claude AI models and products, which have fueled its meteoric rise this year. Anthropic said in its prospectus that it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up a staggering 1,200% from the same period last year. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company in 2021 after he and a small group of researchers defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. Anthropic has faced sharp criticism over its positions on safety, regulation and national security, including by President Donald Trump and other senior government officials. CNBC's reporters are covering Anthropic's IPO live on air and online from our bureaus in San Francisco and Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey, and from the Nasdaq in New York City. Wall Street banks are set to reap a huge windfall from Anthropic's IPO, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley among the biggest earners. The company disclosed in its latest SEC filing that it agreed to pay the banks $550 million, surpassing the roughly $500 million payday banks took in from SpaceX's IPO in June. Anthropic's investors and other partners are taking a victory lap upon the AI lab's successful debut. Investors Menlo Ventures and Lightspeed dedicated the front page of their websites to congratulating Anthropic, as did counsel Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati . Bessemer's Byron Deeter posted a thread on X detailing the backstory of the firm's investment in Anthropic. Menlo Ventures partner Matt Murphy, an early Anthropic investor, said the firm's aggregate position in the AI company is around $25 billion. "Clearly the most epic return for Menlo Ventures in our history, and one of the top handful in the history of venture capital," Murphy told CNBC in an interview. "We feel grateful. We have over five LPs that we've delivered over a billion dollars of returns to, and at the end of the day, that's really our job." Ashton Kutcher congratulated Dario Amodei and "the whole team at Anthropic" in a post on X shortly before the AI company's first trade. Kutcher co-founded Sound Ventures , a Los Angeles-based venture capital firm, which invested in Anthropic in 2023 and participated in several subsequent funding rounds. The VC firm also counts Guy Oseary, the legendary talent manager for musicians including Madonna, among its cofounders. Bloomberg reported that Sound Ventures owns roughly half a percent of Anthropic, citing sources familiar with the matter. Sound Ventures' stake is likely now worth billions of dollars after the company's lofty IPO. Byron Deeter, a partner at Bessemer Venture Partners, called Anthropic 's IPO a " Google moment" for the frontier lab during CNBC's Halftime Report. At over $2 trillion in market capitalization, Anthropic has entered Google's ranks as one of the most valuable companies in the world, behind Apple , Microsoft , Nvidia , Alphabet (Google's parent company), and Amazon . But Deeter says Anthropic doesn't need to "dominate intelligence" in the same way that Google dominates search. The artificial intelligence ecosystem will see "multiple great businesses," Deeter says, adding that he expects Anthropic to continue to be a market leader while also pacing the frontier of AI model development. Anthropic has an unusual governance structure . The company is a public benefit corporation, which means it's required to balance the financial interest of stockholders, the best interests of those affected by its conduct and its "company purpose." Anthropic said in its prospectus that its purpose is to facilitate the "responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity." Anthropic's seven co-founders also wield a lot of power over the company. Prior to the completion of its offering, Anthropic issued a single share of Class F common stock to a limited liability company called "Founder LLC." Anthropic's co-founders are the sole members of Founder LLC, and the entity holds 50.1% of the voting power of the company's outstanding shares. Each co-founder sold 3.38 million shares in the IPO, according to the prospectus, for total proceeds of $1.96 billion. Additionally, Anthropic introduced an independent governance body called the " Long-Term Benefit Trust " in 2023, which has the authority to elect and remove the majority of the company's board of directors. Anthropic opened with a market capitalization of nearly $2.01 trillion, behind only Apple , Microsoft , Nvidia , Alphabet and Amazon . Ben Bernanke, the former chair of the Federal Reserve , is in the room at the Nasdaq as investors celebrate Anthropic's first trade. Anthropic in July appointed Bernanke to its Long-Term Benefit Trust, the AI company's independent governance structure that advises it and appoints its board members. Anthropic shares popped 34% in the company's Nasdaq debut. Anthropic is indicated to open at $111 per share, a person familiar told CNBC. Anthropic is indicated to open at $110 a share, a person familiar told CNBC. Amodei told JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon in a fireside chat on Friday that he thinks talent and culture are the "most important things" that drive a company's success, which is why he and his co-founders have tried to place so much emphasis on those areas at Anthropic. Anthropic requires every employee to pass a culture interview, which is taken very seriously, Amodei said. sources.title: Google gives Gemini the ability to use your Mac for you
sources.text: Google on Thursday announced that it is bringing computer use to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, allowing its AI to complete tasks on users’ behalf, navigating native Mac apps and browsing websites in the background. The tech giant is a little late to the game with this launch, as other leading AI model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta have already been offering agentic features in their desktop applications for some time. Meanwhile, Google only this week announced the broader rollout of Gemini’s “Tasks,” the in-app feature that allows the AI to work more as an agent, helping users sign into websites, make online purchases, or book appointments. Google also only recently began admitting early testers to try its revamped “CC” AI agent, announced in September , which is designed to help families stay organized across email, calendars, chats, and tasks. Computer use is another type of agentic offering that allows an AI agent being able to take actions directly on the user’s computer — in Gemini’s case, a Mac. This allows the AI to complete multi-step tasks that involve getting things done across the local files, apps, and the web. After the user instructs the AI what they want to do, they’ll see the agent working in a live preview in their chat, while still keeping their screen and cursor free to continue working on other things. As with other AI agents offering computer use, users can pause, stop, and approve Gemini’s actions before they happen. Google suggests the feature could be useful for tedious tasks and other workflows, like filling out forms, repeating the same task over and over across a batch of files, organizing files into folders based on specific criteria, creating slideshows from files or information in online dashboards, and more. The feature is initially available in English in the U.S. and requires the Gemini app for Mac and a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription.
